nameStory: The 'perplexed' tick-trefoil gets its name from the decades of confusion it caused botanists! When first described in 1950, this species was so similar to its cousin, the tall tick-trefoil, that scientists remained baffled about how to tell them apart until 2020. The 'tick-trefoil' part comes from its sticky seed pods that cling to clothing and fur like tiny ticks.
description: Perplexed tick-trefoil is a native wildflower in the legume family, related to beans and peas. This herbaceous perennial produces small pink to purple flowers arranged in loose clusters along upright stems. The plant typically grows 2-4 feet tall with the characteristic three-leaflet leaves (called trifoliate) common to many legumes. Like other tick-trefoils, it's best known for its segmented seed pods that break apart and stick tenaciously to anything that brushes against them.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Flattened, jointed seed pods that break into segments, each covered with tiny hooked hairs that feel scratchy and cling stubbornly to fabric or fur

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Three-part leaves (trifoliate) with oval leaflets that feel smooth on top and slightly fuzzy underneath, arranged alternately up the stem

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small pink to purple pea-like flowers in loose, branching clusters at stem tips, each flower about 1/4 inch long with the irregular shape typical of legumes

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright perennial growing 2-4 feet tall with multiple branching stems that feel somewhat sticky when touched

habitat: Look for perplexed tick-trefoil in open woodlands, woodland edges, and clearings throughout New England. It prefers well-drained soils and partial shade, often growing alongside other woodland wildflowers and shrubs. You'll sometimes find it in old fields that are transitioning back to forest.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges with fresh three-part leaves, but the plant remains relatively inconspicuous during early spring months.
seasonality.summer: Blooming occurs from mid to late summer, with pink-purple flower clusters appearing at stem tips from July through August.
seasonality.fall: Seed pods mature and become increasingly sticky, readily attaching to passing animals and hikers. Leaves may turn yellowish before dropping.
seasonality.winter: Plant dies back to the ground, leaving only the root system alive underground until spring regrowth.

funFact: This plant stumped professional botanists for 70 years! Even though it was officially named in 1950, scientists couldn't reliably tell it apart from tall tick-trefoil until 2020, making it one of the most recently 'solved' plant identification mysteries in North America.
confusionNotes: Perplexed tick-trefoil is extremely difficult to distinguish from tall tick-trefoil (Desmodium glabellum) - so much so that even botanists were confused until very recently. The differences are subtle and technical, involving flower and leaf measurements that require close examination with magnification.
contextualKnowledge: Much of what you'll read about this species in older field guides and websites may be inaccurate due to the long-standing confusion with tall tick-trefoil. Any identification information published before 2020 should be viewed with skepticism, as the two species were routinely misidentified.
compareHints: Among New England's tick-trefoils, perplexed tick-trefoil is most easily confused with tall tick-trefoil, requiring expert examination to separate reliably. It differs from showy tick-trefoil by having smaller flowers in looser clusters, and from the trailing species by its upright growth habit. The sticky, segmented seed pods are the best field mark to confirm you're looking at any tick-trefoil species rather than other legumes.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its tick-trefoil relatives, showy tick-trefoil is typically the tallest and most robust, with the largest and most densely packed flower clusters.

Among New England's many ticktrefoils, panicled ticktrefoil stands out with its distinctly narrow, lance-shaped leaflets - much thinner than the broad leaflets of showy tick-trefoil or the rounded leaves of round-leaved trailing tick-trefoil.
Among the tick-trefoils, this is the only one with perfectly round leaflets and a distinctly trailing growth habit.
Among the tick-trefoils, this species stands out for its height and smooth appearance.
Among New England's tick-trefoils, Maryland tick-trefoil is distinguished by its relatively small, smooth leaflets and delicate overall appearance.
Among its tick-trefoil relatives, little-leaf stands out for its distinctly smaller leaflets and notably hairy stems.
Among its tick-trefoil relatives, the toothed variety stands out for its distinctly serrated leaf edges - most other species have smooth or only slightly toothed leaflets.
Among New England's tick-trefoils, hoary tick-trefoil is the gray ghost - its fuzzy, grayish appearance makes it unmistakable.
Among New England's ticktrefoils, sessileleaf is the only one with leaves that attach directly to the stem without stalks - all its relatives have obvious leaf stems.
Among the tick-trefoils, stiff tick-trefoil stands out for its rigid, unbending stems - most others like showy tick-trefoil or panicled tick-trefoil have flexible stems that sway easily.
